articles.full_text:
In Pictures
Photos: Iran marks US embassy takeover with rallies against US, Israel
Tehran rallies see slogans, flag burnings, and claims of US-Israeli defeats amid historic embassy takeover anniversary.
Iran marked the anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the United States embassy in Tehran on Wednesday with mass rallies in the capital, as officials used the occasion to hail what they called US and Israeli “defeats” in recent elections and on the battlefield.
On November 4, 1979, Iranian students stormed the US embassy, taking 52 American diplomats and citizens hostage for 444 days, a crisis that cemented the rupture between Tehran and Washington, which have had no formal diplomatic relations since.
This year’s anniversary comes against the backdrop of a war launched by the US and Israel against Iran on February 28, in which Iran’s longtime supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed, roiling global energy markets and disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Thousands of demonstrators marched through central Tehran, burning US and Israeli flags and chanting “Death to America” and “Death to Israel”. Effigies and caricatures of US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu were paraded through the streets, including one showing Trump as a ferocious dog held on a leash by Netanyahu.
Tehran Mayor Alireza Zakani told the crowd that the US and Israel had suffered a “decisive defeat”, including in Tuesday’s US congressional midterm elections, which was considered a rebuke of Trump’s Republican Party, claiming US weaknesses were the result of Iranian “steadfastness and strength”.
Iran’s judiciary chief, Gholam Hossein Mohseni Ejehi, echoed the message in a post on X, saying: “Trump failed both in war and in politics. We will certainly impose even more defeats upon him.”

articles.title: Ukrainian strikes kill three in Russia’s Belgorod region
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Russian strikes also cut power to Ukrainian cities as Moscow claims 700 Ukrainian drones downed across multiple regions.
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian strikes kill three in Russia’s Belgorod region
Russian strikes also cut power to Ukrainian cities as Moscow claims 700 Ukrainian drones downed across multiple regions.
Ukrainian drone strikes have killed three people in Russia’s Belgorod region, while attacks cut power to multiple cities in Ukraine and parts of Russian-occupied Crimea, officials reported.
Local Russian authorities in Belgorod, which borders Ukraine, announced the three deaths on Wednesday. In Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia’s overnight attacks damaged power generation facilities and substations in nine regions leaving emergency outages in many cities.

Russia’s Defence Ministry confirmed on Telegram that it hit two power stations in Ukraine’s Kyiv and Zhytomyr regions. Ukraine has repeatedly said Moscow is targeting its energy grid as temperatures drop before winter.
Overnight, Russian attacks on critical infrastructure caused hours-long power and water outages across Kyiv and surrounding regions.
Residents in the capital were urged to use public drinking water fountains, and emergency centres offering hot tea and power points to charge devices were set up in the worst-hit areas.
There were also power outages in Crimea, the peninsula Russia seized from Ukraine in 2014, home to approximately 2.5 million residents. Russia’s Ministry of Energy said Ukrainian strikes hit energy infrastructure overnight and that temporary outage schedules were in force. It did not say how many households were affected.
But reports also indicated that Russia-held Crimea ordered power cuts after an accident outside the region, a Moscow-installed official said, according to the Reuters news agency.
In addition to the capital, Kyiv, Russia also hit the regions of Poltava, Dnipro, Kirovohrad and Rivne, Reuters reported, citing Ukraine’s emergency service and local officials.
In southern Russia, a Ukrainian drone attack started a fire at a major warehouse belonging to Ozon, known as Russia’s Amazon. The strikes were on an Ozon distribution facility in the town of Adygeysk, in the Republic of Adygea, regional head Murat Kumpilov said.
Ozon said all workers were evacuated and no one was hurt, and that it had removed damaged goods from its listings and rerouted deliveries.
Russia’s Defence Ministry also said it downed 709 Ukrainian drones across 14 regions, Crimea and the Black and Azov seas.
Kremlin response to US midterms
Amid ongoing fighting between Russia and Ukraine, Russia’s Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Kremlin hopes United States President Donald Trump will continue his peace efforts after a sweeping Democratic victory in the congressional midterms dealt a blow to the president.
“President Trump continues to exercise his powers. We sincerely hope that he will also continue his peacemaking efforts,” Peskov said in a statement.
Whether a change in Congress could hinder Trump’s peace efforts, Peskov said, as cited by the state-run Interfax news outlet, that it was “an internal matter for America”.
Democratic control of the legislature in January is expected to bring a more vocal pro-Kyiv majority in Congress that could pressure Trump to change tack, but there is little hope that the US will return as a major financial backer of Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Zelenskyy awarded US First Lady Melania Trump the Order of Princess Olga, which honours women who have contributed to Ukraine, according to a presidential decree on Wednesday.
The decree noted Melania Trump’s “significant personal contribution” in providing support for humanitarian aid and children in Ukraine.
Ukrainian officials say the US first lady played a pivotal role in organising a six-day local ceasefire to evacuate civilians from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, which ended on Sunday.

articles.title: The Pentagon needs more ammo for the Iran war. Small communities are paying the price.
articles.snippet: From polluted waterways to repeated safety violations, the Army’s aging ammunition factories have left a troubling legacy, The War Horse reports.
articles.full_text:
Editor’s note: This article first appeared on The War Horse, an award-winning nonprofit news organization educating the public on military service. Subscribe to their newsletter.
When Hurricane Helene ripped up the East Coast in the fall of 2024, water from the New River flooded towns and destroyed bridges across parts of West Virginia, North Carolina, and Virginia.
In Radford, Virginia, floodwaters crested at 31 feet. Just downstream, the river surged into the Radford Army Ammunition Plant, tearing through warehouse doors and washing out more than a dozen storage containers with thousands of gallons of toxic chemicals inside.
The Army didn’t warn residents until weeks later about the containers filled with dibutyl phthalate, a key component of rocket propellant that has been linked to cancer and reproductive problems in humans — along with hundreds of gallons of diesel fuel and more than 100,000 pounds of wastewater contaminated with calcium sulfate — that had been washed away in the flood. Officials said later that they assumed the containers would sink to the bottom of the river and floodwaters would dilute any chemical leakage.
At least one container, however, washed up on nearby land, where it was partially drained. Two years later, three remain unaccounted for, according to the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality, which found that more than 1,500 gallons had leaked into the environment.
Radford Army Ammunition Plant had already been cited earlier in 2024 for discharging excessive levels of pollutants into the New River. It faced a similar penalty in 2023. And in 2022, Virginia environmental regulators listed Radford as the state’s top releaser of toxins.
“They’re constantly being cited for putting excessive levels of lead into the water, or other toxic releases into the air, or burning more chemicals than they’re supposed to,” said Alyssa Carpenter, a founder of Citizens for Arsenal Accountability, which advocates for stronger environmental practices at Radford.
Radford is also a critical part of the nation’s munitions supply chain: It is the only domestic producer of certain types of propellant used in artillery and rockets. As the Pentagon moves to replenish its depleted munitions stockpile and increase production, it is relying in part on a network of aging Army ammunition plants like Radford, several of which have long histories of violating environmental and safety regulations.
Advocates say the military has too often treated those risks as secondary to production, leaving workers and nearby communities to absorb the consequences.
“The track record of the Department of Defense agencies is not good,” said Mathy Stanislaus, who helped oversee toxic cleanup efforts at the Environmental Protection Agency during the Obama administration. “It’s always defense. ‘That’s our mission.’ Everything else is secondary.”
Now, advocates worry that pressure to produce more ammunition could intensify the risk to local communities. They argue that the costs of rebuilding America’s arsenal are being borne disproportionately by plant workers and the mostly rural communities surrounding the facilities.
“It’s cheap for the military, but it is very expensive for us, for our entire lives,” Carpenter said. “You can’t increase production without increasing the toxic byproducts that come from that production.”
An Aging Arsenal
As the United States entered World War II, the Army built a network of ammunition plants across the country that became part of Franklin Roosevelt’s “arsenal of democracy.” Many were decommissioned after the war and more closed by the end of the Cold War.
Today, much of the defense industrial base is run by private companies, but the Army still manages a network of specialized arsenals, ammunition plants, and maintenance depots, many of which help manufacture, test, and repair missiles, heavy ordnance, and their components, handling work that ranges from creating raw explosive chemicals and rocket propellant to loading warheads and artillery shells.
The United States military is running low on several critical munitions. A report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies published this summer estimated that U.S. inventory of Patriot interceptor missiles had fallen from more than 2,300 at the start of the Iran War to around 800 by the end of July. Stocks of THAAD interceptors, which shoot down incoming ballistic missiles, had likewise fallen by nearly half, from roughly 450 before the war.
The strain predates the Iran War, however. U.S. inventories of precision-guided weapons and heavy conventional ordnance stockpiles had already been under pressure from decades of post-Cold War factory consolidation and shipments to allies overseas.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the United States produced about 14,000 155 mm artillery shells a month. At times, Ukrainian soldiers were burning through that many rounds in just a few days.
And historically, munitions production has often lost out to other priorities in Pentagon budget fights.
“When you’re putting together a budget, you can’t just ask for everything,” said Carlton Haelig, who works on defense strategy at the Center for a New American Security. “When there need to be cuts to pay for an extra squadron [of fighter jets] purchased, another set of transport aircraft, surface ships, whatever, the place that is often considered for making those cuts is in the munitions portfolio.”
In recent years, however, concern about a potential confrontation with China has pushed the Pentagon to expand munitions production. Last year, the Defense Department established a new council tasked with dramatically increasing production of 14 weapons systems, and it has poured billions of dollars toward accelerating production of 155 mm artillery shells.
Environmental advocates worry that pushing more production through aging Army facilities could worsen existing problems with pollution, worker safety, and transparency.
“Measured by the number of sites where hazardous substances have been released into the environment, the military is far and away the largest polluter in the United States,” said Lenny Siegel, an expert on military contamination who leads the Center for Public Environmental Oversight. “I see the simple issue of math. If you’re releasing X into the environment now, you’re going to release 10X when you multiply your production by 10.”
Justine Barati, a spokesperson for the Army Sustainment Command, which oversees these facilities, disagreed.
“The U.S. Army does not, and will never, compromise the safety of our workforce or our surrounding communities to meet production quotas. Protecting our people and the environment is foundational to national security,” she said. “We cannot sustain warfighter readiness without safe, resilient, and compliant installations.”
Barati pointed to a sweeping $18 billion modernization effort across these facilities, saying the Army’s “highest priority” in the modernization is to improve environmental compliance and workplace safety.
But that project is not scheduled to be completed until 2038, and the Army is already accelerating production at some facilities.
“At the same time, the Ukraine war started to get hot and heavy, and we were given the edict that’s like, ‘hurry up and go fast’,” Maj. Gen. John Reim, head of the joint armaments and ammunitions program executive office, told Breaking Defense last year.
EPA records show that all the Army ammunition plants and arsenals involved in producing, testing, or storing weapon components have been cited or flagged for noncompliance by the EPA or state regulators in the past five years. Four of them have been flagged for “significant noncompliance” by the EPA, designating them severe or chronic violators of environmental law. Many of them have also violated state environmental regulations.
EPA records show Scranton Army Ammunition Plant in Pennsylvania, for instance, which helps forge steel 155 mm shell bodies, was flagged for violating the Clean Water Act and Clean Air Act multiple times during 2024 and 2025. At the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in 2023, regulators found workers improperly detonated explosives in a detonation chamber, among other issues. At Holston Army Ammunition Plant in Kingsport, Tennessee, BAE Systems, which operates the plant, was fined this October by the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation’s air pollution control division for improper record-keeping and reporting of data.
Federal and state regulators can inspect and penalize these facilities, but the fines are often small compared with the sheer size and resources of the Defense Department. After EPA inspectors found alleged violations at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, in 2024, the EPA fined the Army and plant operator American Ordnance just under $40,000 — compare that with a $53 million Army contract American Ordnance was awarded this year for its work at the plant.
“The biggest problem is that the Department of Defense is effectively self-regulating,” Stanislaus, the former EPA official, said.
“When the rubber hits the road, EPA and state agencies simply do not have the authority to mandate certain activities, everything from preventing harm to doing the cleanup.”
A Whistleblower’s Safety Concerns
The fire that erupted on a July night in Crane, Indiana, burned for 15 hours.
Workers at Crane Army Ammunition Activity, which disposes of old munitions, had been storing mortar rounds outdoors in wooden crates beneath a tarp in the baking sun. Temperatures had climbed into the high 90s for several days.
The rounds contained red phosphorus, which can generate heat and flammable gases as it degrades. On the evening of July 6, 2022, nearly 115,000 pounds of red phosphorus ignited, sending flames and smoke billowing into the sky.
What happened before and after illustrates how difficult it can be to hold these facilities accountable.
Three years earlier, Rick Ward, the newly hired safety chief at Crane Army Ammunition Activity, which is housed at Naval Weapons Station Crane, had concerns with safety at the facility. A safety program for controlling hazardous substances was not fully implemented. Hazardous processes weren’t properly classified. Slings used to move heavy explosives didn’t have current certifications.
Ward pointed to an earlier explosion at Crane, in 2013, that sent five people to the hospital. An OSHA inspection afterward identified three dozen safety violations, and an Army “lessons learned” report cited a lack of clear safety procedures.
Ward worried that the safety culture at Crane hadn’t changed. He began bringing concerns up with his supervisors, according to documents he shared with The War Horse.
“Can you imagine taking over as a safety director and knowing that you’ve been handed 36 OSHA violations that never got corrected?” he said.
The year before Ward arrived, EPA had also cited Naval Weapons Station Crane — the base where Crane Army Ammunition Activity is housed — for improperly storing hazardous waste. But Ward felt his concerns were not being taken seriously. So in 2020, he filed an anonymous complaint with OSHA.
Because of COVID-related restrictions, OSHA asked the Army to investigate the allegations itself. Ironically, Crane leaders assigned Ward to conduct the investigation.
About an hour after Ward submitted his report, he said, he was put on administrative leave. He was fired several months later, according to a statement from his lawyers.
Ward has struggled to find work ever since. Crane barred him from the installation, and the Air Force, where he serves as a reserve officer, revoked his security clearance.
“It’s really hard to get a job when you’ve been on the front page of every newspaper in Indiana,” he said.
Barati, the Army Sustainment Command spokesperson, disputed Ward’s account.
“The Army did not retaliate against Mr. Rick Ward in any form or manner. The Army takes workplace safety very seriously and welcomes safety concern feedback from all our employees,” she said.
Many of Ward’s concerns were later substantiated.
A whistleblower investigation partially or fully upheld five of his eight allegations. Among them: Crane did not maintain an accurate list of locations where hazardous work occurred and lacked a complete safety plan for controlling and handling hazardous substances.
EPA inspections in 2023 and 2024 found additional problems at Naval Weapons Station Crane. Inspectors reported materials were still stored in ways that could create fire risks, hazardous materials lacked proper labeling, open containers held corrosive waste, and hazardous waste was kept onsite for more than three times the legal time limit.
“If you mislabel a particular compound, and you put it into a vessel that cannot handle the corrosiveness of that, then it leaks through that vessel and contaminates the ground,” Stanislaus said. “Terrible things can happen.”
Last fall, EPA notified Naval Weapons Station Crane that it planned to assess nearly $250,000 in penalties for the violations.
That is a significant EPA penalty. But for Crane, it’s barely a line item in the budget.
Toxins in the Air
Not long after Alyssa Carpenter graduated from Virginia Tech in 2017, just a few miles from the Radford Army Ammunition Plant, she had to have her thyroid removed. She was 26, otherwise healthy, and had no family history of thyroid cancer. Doctors told her the gland was covered in suspicious nodules.
Carpenter cannot say for sure what caused her condition. But as a student at Virginia Tech, she had advocated for better environmental controls at the plant, and she worries the chemicals the plant releases into the environment may have played a role in her illness.
For decades, Radford and other military facilities have disposed of old munitions and production waste by burning or detonating them in the open, releasing toxic gases, particulate matter, and volatile organic compounds into the air.
The United States generally banned open burning and open detonation of hazardous waste in 1980 but created an exception for explosive waste that could not safely be treated another way. That exception has allowed the practice to continue at military and civilian munition facilities.
In 2025, 45 years after the ban, 64 public and private facilities across the United States were still allowed to burn or detonate hazardous waste.
Residents around Radford have long raised concerns about thyroid disease in the area, though a 2022 review of cancer-registry data by VPM News, a local NPR station, found mixed evidence of unusually high rates. What is clear is that the plant regularly releases hazardous pollutants into the air. According to EPA data, in 2024, Radford released into the air — along with other chemicals — 19,000 pounds of ammonia, which reacts with the atmosphere to create a fine particulate matter known to cause respiratory distress, and more than 900 pounds of lead compounds or lead, a neurotoxin with no known safe level of human exposure. EPA requires facilities to report lead emissions if they exceed just 100 pounds a year.
Barati, the Army Sustainment Command spokesperson, said that Radford had reduced the amount of waste treated by open burning by more than 50% since 2017. She also pointed to a new energetic waste incinerator under construction at the facility that will ultimately replace the need for open burning. The incinerator, originally scheduled to be completed in 2025, will not be operational until 2027, Barati said.
Open burns are subject to environmental limits, and facilities are supposed to account for wind patterns and other factors to make burns safer. But those safeguards can be difficult to enforce.
At Crane, for instance, EPA inspectors cited the facility in 2023 for conducting burns when its own records showed weather conditions outside permitted limits. (Crane officials told the EPA weather was recorded at a different time of day and that the weather was in parameters when it conducted the burns).
Technology has changed since the U.S. allowed an exception for the open burning or detonation of military munitions in 1980. Many other countries, including Germany and Canada, have banned open burning and open detonation of hazardous waste, and military munitions are disposed of in contained burn chambers or closed incinerators. In 2024, the EPA proposed new rules that would further restrict the practice and push facilities toward safer alternative technologies. But the rulemaking has stalled. An EPA spokesperson told The War Horse that the agency plans to finalize the regulations by the end of this year.
The military has moved away from open-air waste burning in recent years at overseas bases.
For decades, troops stationed in Iraq, Afghanistan, and other countries burned everything from medical waste and plastics to old explosives in open burn pits. Military officials defended the pits as a practical necessity in remote war zones.
Like the residents of some communities near ammunition plants in the U.S., service members at bases with burn pits breathed in toxic air containing particulate matter that irritated their throats and lungs, and heavy metals that accumulated in their tissues. When they came home from deployment, they began developing rare cancers and other diseases.
But as veterans reported respiratory illnesses, cancers, and other health problems after breathing in the smoke, public pressure grew. The military eventually curtailed the use of burn pits overseas, and Congress passed the PACT Act in 2022, expanding VA benefits for millions of veterans exposed to the toxic substances during military service — but there are no such benefits for civilians exposed to domestic burn pits.
For Carpenter, that history shows the military can change when the risks become impossible to ignore.
“If it’s toxic for service members, then it’s going to be toxic for community members as well,” she said.
This article from The War Horse was edited by Paul Szoldra, fact-checked by Jess Rohan, and copy-edited by Mitchell Hansen-Dewar.

articles.title: Saildrone expands its European market reach with manufacturing partner in Norway
articles.snippet: CEO Tom Fidjeland told reporters at the Euronaval trade show here that taking on the work of churning out Surveyors was “technically not difficult,” with a first mold already being readied.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — U.S.-based naval drone maker Saildrone has picked Norwegian naval builder Umoe Mandal to produce the Surveyor multipurpose surveillance craft locally, with an eye on new sales in Northern Europe, company executives said.
The Norwegian shipbuilder, headquartered on the country’s southern tip reaching into the North Sea, specializes in composite structures for the naval sector, including masts for British Type 26 frigates. CEO Tom Fidjeland told reporters at the Euronaval trade show here that taking on the work of churning out Surveyors was “technically not difficult,” with a first mold already being readied.
“Mandal’s role in producing the Surveyor will strengthen Europe’s maritime defense industrial base and support the delivery of sovereign maritime domain awareness capabilities to Northern European navies,” Saildrone said in a statement.
The U.S. company will provide its autonomy suite, navigation, electronics and surveillance technology to be mounted on the Norwegian-built Surveyor bodies, the plan goes.
The Surveyor drone is 20 meters long, powered by a diesel motor and wind — a sail-like structure 13 meters high that also houses the onboard electronics. Saildrone markets the vehicle, which can be left alone cruising the ocean for up to 100 days, as a data collector on adversaries and maritime conditions. Multiple drones can be networked to increase the coverage area, according to the manufacturer.
Saildrone’s lineup also includes the smaller Explorer and Voyager models, as well we the larger Spectre, a weapons-capable version still in development.
The partnership comes as the U.S. company has positioned itself to sell naval drones to European navies keen on policing their territorial waters, including in the Baltic and North seas as well as Arctic locales.
Saildrone’s managing director for Europe, Robert Kleist, cited an alliance of Northern European nations Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden, NORDEFCO for short, as a potential business generator for naval drones. The pact entails an acquisition track that could spin out national task orders for unmanned platforms, for which Saildrone would then compete, Kleist said.
Umoe Mandall CEO Fidjeland said his company will build a new production site near its main plant devoted to cranking out Surveyors, with an initial production rate of at least two per month.
In October, Saildrone announced a yearlong maritime surveillance mission involving four Voyager drone for the Swedish Navy. Denmark, which straddles the North and Baltic seas, a key transit route for Russian warships heading to the open Atlantic, has been using the craft since 2025.
Saildrone announced a European headquarters in Copenhagen in August, noting plans for an expanded drone production footprint in Europe. Besides Norway, those entail making Spectre boats in the Netherlands at yacht maker Van Der Valk Shipyard, and Surveyor wings in Poland, Saildrone founder and CEO Richard Jenkins said then.

articles.title: Babcock launches digital platform to link warship construction and fleet support
articles.snippet: U.K-based Babcock International has launched Pelorus, a digital platform intended to connect warship construction, operations and maintenance data.
articles.full_text:
VIENNA — U.K-based Babcock International has launched Pelorus, a digital platform intended to connect warship construction, operations and maintenance data.
The British defense and engineering company announced the launch Nov. 3 at the Euronaval defense trade show in Paris, saying the platform already operates in selected Babcock-managed maritime construction and support environments. Babcock did not identify the deployments or customers involved, or provide figures showing how the platform has affected fleet availability or maintenance costs.
According to the company, Pelorus combines information from multiple systems to track shipbuilding progress, commissioning and trials, fleet availability, maintenance and logistics.
“The future of maritime capability depends on the ability to connect design, production, operational and support data into a single digital environment,” said Nick Hine, Babcock’s chief growth officer and marine chief executive, in the announcement.
The company positioned the platform as supporting both existing fleets and future combinations of crewed and autonomous vessels, linking it to its ARMOR Force concept − short for Autonomous and Remote, Maritime Operational Response Force. Babcock said Pelorus could also be adapted for other defense and critical infrastructure applications.
Babcock’s naval business spans shipbuilding and long-term fleet support. The company is building five Type 31 frigates for Britain’s Royal Navy at its Rosyth yard in Scotland. It also maintains and upgrades British nuclear-powered submarines at Devonport and Clyde, according to its website.

articles.title: France tasks Naval Group to develop large oceangoing underwater drone
articles.snippet: France signed a contract with shipbuilder Naval Group to develop an operational demonstrator of a large-sized oceangoing underwater drone, with sea trials to start in 2028.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — France signed a contract with shipbuilder Naval Group to develop an operational demonstrator of a large-sized oceangoing underwater drone, with sea trials to start in 2028.
The demonstrator of the uncrewed combat underwater vehicle, or UCUV, will have to show both endurance and autonomous decision-making capability, the French Armed Forces ministry said late Tuesday. The vehicle will be capable of carrying out missions ranging from intelligence gathering, surveillance and reconnaissance to “more offensive neutralization actions,” the ministry said.
For the French Navy, a plus-sized oceangoing autonomous underwater vehicle could offer a way to extend its presence across the country’s vast maritime space. France has the world’s second-largest exclusive economic zone behind the United States, with about 11 million square kilometers spread across the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans.
“In the face of intensifying competition for underwater domains and threats weighing on critical infrastructure, the start of development of the UCUV demonstrator is a strong marker of the French Navy’s determination to establish its technological and tactical superiority,” the ministry said.
“France thus joins the very select group of nations engaged in the definition and development of a large-sized unmanned underwater vehicle capability.”
The U.S. Navy has been working with Boeing to develop the Orca uncrewed underwater vehicle, while the United Kingdom last month said it fired a heavy torpedo from an extra-large uncrewed underwater vessel for the first time. Australia in September said it was buying a fleet of Ghost Shark extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicles from Anduril for A$1.7 billion (US$1.2 billion).
The agreement between France’s Defense Innovation Agency and Naval Group follows an initial market study started in 2023 with the Directorate General for Armament, the ministry said. The demonstrator must be air transportable, and able to be deployed from a pier or a surface vehicle, it said.
Naval Group has previously developed a 10-ton ocean-going drone demonstrator using its own money, and the yard’s self-funded work allowed for rapid evaluation of the technology required for the UCUV project, the ministry said. France in January 2024 said it ordered a technological demonstrator based on the prototype to test energy autonomy, sensor integration and autonomous operation.
The future ocean-going demonstrator will be equipped with a “controlled autonomous decision-making system” that will allow the underwater drone to adapt to tactical situations, the environment and potential breakdowns, either by itself or in collaboration with other systems, the ministry said.
France’s 2026 defense budget allocated €30 million in commitment authorizations and €17 million in payment appropriations for an ocean-going underwater drone demonstrator. The country’s 2024-2030 defense programming law including €5 billion for drones and robots over the seven-year period, including underwater drones.
The sea trials will validate the technological choices for the demonstrator as well as provide a better understanding of the operational response to new forms of naval combat, the ministry said.

articles.title: Naval Group unveils new drone carrier concept
articles.snippet: “The return of high-intensity conflict and the emergence of hybrid naval warfare require a new vision. Naval Group answers with a new concept ship: SCX 26,” the company stated.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — French shipbuilder Naval Group has unveiled an 8,000-ton drone carrier concept designed to deploy fleets of surface, aerial and underwater drones.
“The return of high-intensity conflict and the emergence of hybrid naval warfare require a new vision. Naval Group answers with a new concept ship: SCX 26,” Naval Group wrote in a Tuesday post on X.
Still in its blueprint stage, the company unveiled its concept at the Euronaval defense show in Paris. Naval Group said in a press release that it developed the carrier based on new operational requirements, lessons learned from recent wars, and medium- to long-term technological advancements.
The idea is for the carrier to be what the French group calls an “operational hub of a hybrid fleet,” able to launch a variety of drones for missions ranging from intelligence gathering to anti-submarine warfare.
According to the theoretical capabilities outlined, the ship would measure 170 meters in length and weigh 8,000 tons, with a crew of 150. The carrier is expected to reach a maximum of 30 knots and roam the seas for more than 8,000 nautical miles. Naval Group plans for the ship’s core onboard weapon to be composed of “over 100 vertical launching system silos of various classes and an electromagnetic gun capable of rapid fire.”
Separately, the French shipbuilder on Tuesday also signed a contract with the French Armament General Directorate (DGA) to begin manufacturing an unmanned combat underwater vehicle (UCUV) demonstrator intended for the French Navy.
While the project was officially launched in 2023, Naval Group since 2016 has self-funded the development of this extra-large underwater drone. During a nine-month study in 2023, the company said it tested Controlled Decision-Making Autonomy, an “onboard brain” algorithm that coordinates mission parameters and enables unmanned systems to autonomously execute challenging operations while adhering to human-defined mission boundaries.
The UCUV demonstrator’s first sea testing is slotted for 2028 to “validate a mid-term operational response” to new areas of conflict, Naval Group said.

articles.title: MBDA’s high-speed strike missile to have range ‘far’ exceeding Exocet
articles.snippet: Stratus RS, for rapid strike, is being developed for France and the United Kingdom, and MBDA is awaiting a development contract from France’s Directorate General for Armament.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — MBDA targets a range for its future high-speed strike missile Status RS that will be “far, far, far” more than of the Exocet anti-ship missile with its more than 200-kilometer range, said Olivier Gauffin, the company’s deputy director for sales and business development, at a briefing at the Euronaval maritime-defense exhibition on Tuesday.
The high supersonic missile will cover four missions, including deep strike and anti-ship strike, suppression and destruction of enemy air defenses, as well as strikes against large aircraft including airborne warning systems and tankers, Gauffin said.
Stratus RS, for rapid strike, is being developed for France and the United Kingdom, and MBDA is awaiting a development contract from France’s Directorate General for Armament on behalf of the two partners. The company is simultaneously working on a stealthy subsonic cruise missile with a larger warhead called Stratus LO, for low observable, on behalf of France, the U.K. and Italy.
“The goal is very clear, it’s to face the threat of the decades to come, and we have two options to do it, which are complementary,” Gauffin said. “One is more a Ferrari, and the other is more a truck, a stealth truck.”
NATO has called on allies in Europe to rebuild offensive capabilities, as the alliance faces an aggressive Russia on its eastern flank. Stratus RS in particular would fill a gap in the inventory of European militaries, which mostly lack weapons able to destroy enemy air defenses.
The high-speed missile will be able to combine very low or very high trajectories to defeat hard-to-destroy targets such as frigates and destroyers or ground-based air defense systems, according to Gauffin. The missile will have a liquid ramjet engine that can be throttled, and will be highly maneuverable, the MBDA executive said.
Stratus RS will have a radio-frequency seeker combined with synthetic aperture radar, which provides the missile with a land-attack and a top-attack capability, according to Gauffin, who said Thales is providing the seeker technology. The idea for the slower, stealthy missile is to have only passive radio-frequency and infrared sensors, and no radar.
While the equipment in the Stratus RS missile will be new, it will be based on technology MBDA uses in other missiles, the executive said. The company has already done “a lot of trials” around the critical components, including propulsion, seeker, warhead and data management, and full development of the missile is expected to start “very soon,” Gauffin said.
MBDA uses ramjet technology in its Meteor air-to-air missile.
Both Stratus missiles will be able to be air-launched from platforms including Dassault Aviation’s Rafale jet, the Eurofighter Typhoon as well as the future aircraft being developed as part of the British-Italian-Japanese Global Combat Air Programme, with a size and mass “very close” to the Storm Shadow cruise missile. The missiles will use a booster for launch from ships or land.
MBDA expects flight testing of both Stratus missiles to start before the end of the decade, with the missiles to enter in service at the beginning of the 2030s.
The size of the Stratus RS means it’s not compatible with NATO-standard size torpedo tubes, meaning the missile is not envisaged as being submarine launched, according to Gauffin. For vertical launch, the missile would require a new, wider version of Naval Group’s Sylver vertical launch system, though Gauffin said there would be no change to the shipborne space occupied by the VLS.
The company also presented details on a new version of its Naval Cruise Missile, with production to start in early 2030. The updated version will be more resistant to satellite-navigation jamming, with increased survivability and new sensors, and keep the same size but with increased range and lethality, said Sophie Bourdais, vice-president for strike at MBDA.
Bourdais declined to provide specifics on the range of the Naval Cruise Missile in either its current or future iteration, other than to say it is more than 1,000 km.
The updated missile will also benefit from new mission-preparation software called Fastrike that cuts target planning down to minutes from hours, according to Bourdais. MBDA plans to integrate the capability in the Storm Shadow/Scalp EG cruise missile and the current version of the Naval Cruise Missile before 2030, the executive said.
The Naval Cruise Missile was presented as part of the European Long-range Strike Approach, and there is interest from a number of countries in the land-based variant MBDA has developed.
MBDA is still waiting for a development contract from the DGA for the updated Naval Cruise Missile. The production line for the missile in France is inactive but remains in place, and can be restarted to produce the updated version, according to Bourdais.

articles.title: US Air Force asks industry for new cruise missile for Ukraine
articles.snippet: The U.S. Air Force is looking for contractors to mass produce the Extended Range Attack Munition for Ukraine.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Air Force is asking the defense industry whether it can deliver a new cruise missile intended for Ukraine.
Potential contractors are asked to detail their capabilities to provide the Extended Range Attack Munition, a small, air-launched standoff missile intended for mass production.
The Air Force’s new Request For Information, which has a deadline of Nov. 19, offers some technical specifications for ERAM. It should be a 500-pound class weapon with a range of greater than 250 nautical miles and a speed of more than Mach 0.6. Terminal accuracy should be within 10 meters of the target even amid jamming, such as degraded GPS. In addition to blast and fragmentation effects, the weapon should also be capable of limited penetration on impact.
The Air Force describes ERAM as a next-generation cruise missile “designed to provide affordable mass to the fight,” and which “delivers a precision-guided, stand-off capability against high-value fixed targets.”
ERAM is part of the Pentagon’s push for cheaper weapons developed more quickly. In 2024, the Air Force awarded a contract to two small defense companies — Zone 5 Technologies and CoAspire — to develop ERAM prototypes. In January 2026 — less than a year and a half later, the Air Force conducted a live warhead test at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida.
Similar haste can be seen in the RFI, which states that companies should begin delivering the first of more than 1,000 ERAMs no later than three months after the contract is awarded. Deliveries should be complete within 15 months.
One question is whether Ukraine is already using ERAM on its American-made F-16 fighters. In August 2025, the Trump administration announced an $825 million sale of 3,350 ERAMs to Ukraine. In June 2026, Ukrainian media suggested that Ukraine has used the AGM-188A Rusty Dagger — an ERAM version — against the Voronezh Semiconductor Plant, which makes components for Russian missiles.
Another question is to what extent the U.S. military will make use of ERAM. The Air Force published the original RFI in January 2024, nearly two years into the Ukraine War — and nearly two years before the Iran war depleted U.S. inventories of expensive missiles.

articles.title: Defense contractors to demo cargo drones for US Marine Corps
articles.snippet: An event early next year in Huntsville, Alabama, will allow contractors to display their solutions for a Marine battlefield cargo drone.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Marine Corps and Navy will be conducting a technology demonstration for a Marine battlefield cargo drone early next year.
The event, from Jan. 25 to Feb. 5, 2027, in Huntsville, Alabama, will allow contractors to display their drones for the Increment II the Marine Corps’ Tactical Resupply Unmanned Aircraft System, or TRUAS, program.
TRUAS Increment II aims to “provide an organic aerial distribution capability for small-unit logistics support across the last tactical mile in expeditionary advanced base operations and distributed operations,” according to the Monday announcement by the Navy’s Air Warfare Program Management Office, which is sponsoring the demonstration.
Contractors will perform up to five flights, as well as demonstrate ground setup and flight preparation.
The first flight calls for a drone to transport a 100-pound payload up to 40 nautical miles under no-wind conditions, drop off the cargo either automatically or under manual control, and then return to the launch site without refueling. The second flight involves carrying and depositing a payload of 150 pounds or more out to 10 nautical miles.
The UAV must have a speed of at least 50 knots per hour and fly no higher than 1,000 feet during the flights. The UAS must be capable of launch and recovery without mechanical equipment such as a catapult, arresting net or cable.
“Following the two required flights, participants may be given the opportunity to perform up to three additional flights to demonstrate unique features and/or capabilities,” the Navy said.
The announcement lists a variety of technical specifications. They include flying at an altitude of up to 4,500 feet and, eventually, 8,000 feet. Speed should be a minimum of 50 knots per hour, with an eventual goal of 150 knots per hour, in crosswinds of 20 to 30 knots.
The Marine Corps is looking for an unmanned aircraft that can function autonomously, such as assessing the landing zone “before and during landing, day and night, and detect and avoid personnel, equipment, structures, excessive slope, and other terrain hazards.”
With skies becoming saturated by drones, TRUAS craft should have safeguards against collisions, including an “organic airborne sense-and-avoid capability for manned and unmanned aircraft at cruise speed, with performance comparable to a human pilot operating under Visual Flight Rules and sufficient reaction time for collision avoidance.”
The service also anticipates that its cargo drones will be forced to land under enemy fire.
“TRUAS shall minimize the time required to descend from cruise altitude to the LZ [landing zone] to enhance survivability by reducing the window for hostile detection,” the announcement noted.
The announcement did not specify what kind of cargo TRUAS will carry.
Last month, Ukraine claimed to have performed the world’s first drone medevac of a casualty from a frontline position. Ukraine’s 92nd Separate Assault Brigade posted a dramatic video of a wounded soldier being hoisted on a sling attached to the underside of a large hexacopter.
“Heavy Russian drone activity and mined terrain made evacuation by an unmanned ground vehicle impossible,” said Ukrainian media. “Working with the manufacturer, the troops developed a technical solution that allowed the heavy drone to carry the wounded soldier while remaining stable in flight, preventing it from tipping over or swaying excessively.”

articles.title: India taps two domestic shipbuilders for $5.7B corvette program
articles.snippet: India awarded Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers and Goa Shipyard Limited contracts to build five and three corvettes, respectively, for the country’s navy.
articles.full_text:
SINGAPORE — India has signed a contract with two local shipbuilders to build eight Next Generation Corvettes (NGCs) for its navy, the country’s defense ministry announced Monday.
The Indian government awarded Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers Limited (GRSE) and Goa Shipyard Limited (GSL) a contract valued at 53,866.50 crore Indian rupees (approximately US $5.7 billion) to build five and three corvettes, respectively. A crore is a unit in the Indian numbering system equal to 10 million.
The corvettes will feature advanced missiles, weapons and sensor systems, allowing the ships to engage threats in the air, on the surface and underwater, according to the ministry.
“The induction of these ships will significantly enhance the Indian Navy’s operational capabilities in safeguarding maritime trade routes, conducting anti-surface and anti-submarine warfare operations, strengthening coastal defence, undertaking littoral combat operations, and carrying out maritime presence and surveillance missions,” the ministry said in its announcement.
The ministry described the contract award as a “significant milestone,” noting that it marks the first project in which the Indian navy will design the ships and government-owned shipyards — known as Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs) — will build them after being selected through a competitive process.
Both GRSE and GSL are majority owned by the Indian government.
GRSE said in its own announcement that the corvettes “will measure 127 metres in length and 17.6 metres in beam, with a specified deadweight tonnage of 4,950 tonnes” and will be operated by a crew of 150, including 11 officers and 139 sailors.
The company added that the ships will be powered by a combined diesel and gas turbine–cross connect (CODAG-CC) propulsion arrangement driving two controllable-pitch propellers (CPP), giving them a top speed of 26 knots. The ships will be able to remain at sea for up to 14 days without replenishments.
The shipbuilder also provided further details on the corvettes’ planned equipment, stating that they will be armed with indigenous Medium Range Anti-Ship Missiles (MRAShM — although this weapon has also been called the Naval Anti-Ship Missile or NASM-MR), MRSAM medium-range surface-to-air missiles and 324mm torpedo tubes.
Other onboard weapons include the Leonardo 76mm Super Rapid naval gun, Russian AK-360 close-in weapon systems and 12.7mm remote weapon stations.
The corvettes will also feature electro-optical infrared search-and-track systems and multifunction surveillance, tracking and guidance radars — although neither the ministry nor the shipbuilders have identified the specific systems selected.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: House China committee pushes Air Force on think tank cuts
articles.snippet: “Under-resourcing” the China Aerospace Studies Institute (CASI) “could risk undermining the ability of military leaders and civilian policymakers to understand” Beijing’s aerospace strategy and military prowess, according to a letter addressed to Air Force Secretary Troy Meink.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Lawmakers on the House Select Committee on China are pushing the Air Force for answers about a planned downsizing of its Beijing-focused think tank, warning that any reduction in the group’s output could impact America’s national security.
“Under-resourcing” the mission of the China Aerospace Studies Institute (CASI) “could risk undermining the ability of military leaders and civilian policymakers to understand” Beijing’s aerospace strategy and military prowess, according to a copy of the letter viewed exclusively by Breaking Defense.
Addressed to Air Force Secretary Troy Meink and signed by Republican Chairman John Moolenaar and Democratic Ranking Member Ro Khanna, the letter requests a briefing by Nov. 20 to provide “resourcing and personnel decisions” for CASI.
In their letter, House lawmakers say that “[a]ny potential loss” of CASI’s skills “is particularly worrisome” due to China’s burgeoning aerospace capabilities and “aggressive activities in the Indo-Pacific region.” Praising CASI’s work, the lawmakers say that alternatives to the institute’s “in-house expertise” would likely require the Air Force and other government entities “to expend considerable resources to purchase contracted expertise from external vendors.”
Given rapidly advancing air and space power by the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA), the lawmakers say that diminishing relevant analysis is “particularly concerning” and could impact American deterrence, as fears mount over a potential battle for Taiwan.
“As the PLA continues to expand its aerospace capabilities, our need to understand these advancements will continue to grow,” the letter says. An Air Force spokesperson told Breaking Defense that the service “will respond directly to the committee.”
The letter comes after it was revealed in September that the Air Force planned to axe CASI’s 10-member civilian workforce. While the Air Force maintained its premier China-focused think tank would remain open and operate with military personnel, its director, Brendan Mulvaney, stressed in an interview with Breaking Defense that the elimination of its civilian staff would functionally shutter the institute.
Founded by Mulvaney roughly a decade ago, CASI regularly publishes on Beijing’s air and space forces, drawing on open-source information translated from Mandarin. The institute’s publications and training courses are seen as valuable resources for educating the broader military policy community on Chinese air and space power, prompting experts to denounce CASI’s expected downsizing.
“The idea that you could do research or the translations that we’re doing is not credible” without civilian experts, Mulvaney previously told Breaking Defense.
Mulvaney explained that the think tank’s civilian posts are being converted to an unfunded status, meaning that staffers will continue to work until being moved to a different role elsewhere in the Department of the Air Force — and once they leave, their positions cannot be backfilled. CASI’s current commitments stretch until around March and will largely function as usual until then, but after that the institute’s fate becomes more unclear, according to Mulvaney.
News of the CASI cuts raised questions about similar efforts run by the Army, Navy and Marine Corps, though spokespeople for each service previously told Breaking Defense that there are no planned changes for their respective Beijing-focused programs.

articles.title: Shield AI cofounder teases ‘snowball’ of X-BAT fighter drone announcements in Europe
articles.snippet: Ryan Tseng told Breaking Defense that the prospective deals and new industry pacts will be publicized when “we’re ready to announce them.”
articles.full_text:
MUNICH — A “snowball of activities” covering European orders and regional partnership agreements for Shield AI’s X-BAT fighter jet drone are set to be announced “soon,” according to the company’s cofounder and chief strategy officer.
Speaking to Breaking Defense today on the sidelines of the International Fighter Conference, Ryan Tseng said that the prospective deals and new industry pacts will be publicized when “we’re ready to announce them.”
He declined to comment on any aircraft quantities involved in the procurements, saying just “watch this space.”
Europe “can and should be a critical component of the [X-BAT] supply chain for Europe,” he said, noting it would make the region stronger at a “warfighting” level. Additionally, a “European sovereign” supply chain, makes the US more capable, stressed Tseng.
Andrew Hawkes, X-BAT director for Europe at Shield AI, also told Breaking Defense that the company is involved in “several active” sales campaigns for the autonomous, vertical take off and landing (VTOL) aircraft across the continent, though declined to disclose any individual customers.
The planned export business builds off a number of other key, regional developments. In June, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk reportedly said that Shield AI is planning on local production of X-BAT in cooperation with Poland. More recently, the firm announced a “strategic agreement” with Greece’s GEK TERNA, a critical infrastructure investor, based around a potential collaboration on “parts production, aircraft integration and long-term sustainment for X-BAT in Greece.”
Tseng’s assessment on orders comes after the artificial intelligence startup announced on Tuesday that a first, full-scale X-BAT prototype has completed assembly in Frisco, Texas. Next steps will see the aircraft undergo testing at the company’s facility in Newton, Kan., according to a company statement. Shield AI and the US Navy are jointly investing $400 million in X-BAT.
Elsewhere, Tseng said that a per-aircraft cost for the autonomous drone could be brought down to $25 million, but for a higher-end sensor configuration, customers could expect to pay an extra $10 million.
The baseline $25 million figure works out around a quarter “the cost of a Eurofighter or an F-35 in Europe,” he explained. “We think from a lifecycle perspective, it would beat it [in production fighter jets] by a factor of 10″ based on comparable maintenance costs. “You can use far less crew to operate the aircraft” resulting in “savings across the board.”

articles.title: Congress’s defense advocates take big hit in 2026 midterm elections
articles.snippet: A “blue tsunami” of Democrat wins in the midterms has huge implications for the makeup of the congressional defense committees next year.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Democratic wave that swept control of Congress on Tuesday took with it a number of notable defense experts from the House and Senate, with potentially huge consequences for defense policy on Capitol Hill looming.
Results are still flowing in, but Democrats will go into the 120th Congress with at least 228 seats in the House, having picked up 25 so far. NBC News projects that Democrats will ultimately win around 258 seats when all 435 seats have been decided — a decisive margin that gives Democrat leaders in the House a mandate to take bolder legislative action.
Senate races in two states — Alaska and Mississippi — have yet to be called, but as of publication, Democrats have gained seven seats in the upper chamber, taking a 54-44 lead. Even if Democrats take both outstanding seats, the party will lack the 60 votes needed to bypass the filibuster without GOP support.
What does seem clear: Expect major reshufflings of both the House and Senate defense-related committees, thanks to a mix of upsets and retirements.
The so-called “blue tsunami” resulted in a loss for Maine Sen. Susan Collins, chairwoman of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Other GOP lawmakers in the defense world — such as Virginia Rep. Rob Wittman, head of the House Armed Services Committee’s (HASC) tactical air and land subpanel — find themselves still gripped in a competitive fight this morning, with some big defense names in predominantly red states potentially facing a shocking upset.
Meanwhile, Democratic defense leaders — including Rhode Island Sen. Jack Reed, currently the ranking member on the Senate Armed Services Committee, Delaware Sen. Chris Coons, ranking member on the Senate appropriations defense subcommittee, and Washington Rep. Adam Smith, HASC ranking member — all handily won their reelection races and are poised to take over their respective defense committees.
Here’s a breakdown of what happened in the most important defense races:
Maine: Sen. Susan Collins loses to Troy Jackson
Sen. Susan Collins’s 30-year Senate career ended last night after Democrat challenger Troy Jackson emerged victorious in one of the most dramatic races of the midterms.
As chairwoman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Collins is one of the most consequential deciders of the defense budget, having a key role in setting defense and nondefense topline spending levels. Before claiming the gavel, Collins led its defense subcommittee, where she advocated for higher defense budgets and aid for Ukraine. She was one of three Senate Republicans to vote against the confirmation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
ProPublica recently reported that in 2024 the FBI intended to launch a pay-to-play investigation after a former defense contractor told the agency his company had donated to Collins’s political action committee in exchange for winning government contracts in Maine. Collins’s office called the claims “categorically false.”
Jackson is a fifth-generation logger who became the Democratic challenger after Marine Corps veteran Graham Platner withdrew due to allegations of sexual misconduct. He did not make national security issues a centerpiece of his campaign, but listed “No U.S. tax dollars to Israel’s military” as a priority policy on his website.
Virginia: Rep. Rob Wittman vs Shannon Taylor still undecided
The Associated Press has not called the race for Virginia’s 1st Congressional District, but signs don’t look great for Rep. Rob Wittman, who currently sits as chairman of the House Armed Services Committee’s (HASC) Tactical Air and Land Subcommittee.
Wittman faces Democratic challenger Shannon Taylor, a prosecutor who centered her campaign on anti-corruption and affordability, who has already claimed victory. With 98 percent of votes in, Taylor leads by about 2 percent, according to the AP.
If Wittman does survive, he will likely make a play to become the HASC’s top Republican, should current chairman Mike Rogers, R-Ala., not seek a waiver to retain his place on the committee. (Under current House GOP rules, Republicans can only spend three consecutive terms as a committee’s chairperson or ranking member without seeking a waiver.)
Reps. Trent Kelly, who leads the seapower subcommittee, and Ronny Jackson, who leads the intelligence and special operations subcommittee, have also expressed interest in the top GOP spot.
Wittman is highly influential on matters concerning the Air Force and Navy, having previously served as the head of HASC’s Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee. He has championed higher defense spending and larger investments in low-cost attritable weaponry.
California: Rep. Ken Calvert vs. Rep. Young Kim still undecided
The intra-GOP battle for California’s 40th Congressional District is still ongoing, with only about 40 percent of votes recorded at the time of publication. Rep. Ken Calvert, chairman of the House Appropriations defense subcommittee, currently has a 9 percent lead over fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim. (There is no Democratic challenger in this race, as only the top two vote-getters advance from the primary to the general election.)
As the top House defense appropriator, Calvert has endorsed higher defense spending, and has taken particular interest in efforts to increase defense manufacturing and boost Defense Department organizations aimed at bolstering innovation.
Should Calvert emerge victorious in the midterms, he will need to seek a waiver to remain as HAC-D’s top Republican and has indicated he will do so.
Kim, who was first elected to Congress in 2020, does not sit on any of the congressional defense committees. However, she is a member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee as the chairwoman of its East Asia and Pacific subcommittee. She is also a member of the House select committee on China.
Other Key Races:
Rep. Adam Smith defeats Doug Basler: Smith, HASC’s top Democrat, beat Republican challenger Doug Basler for Washington’s 9th Congressional District. With Democrats set to control the House, Smith is poised to once again become HASC chairman.
Rep. Mike Rogers defeats Lee McInnis: The race between HASC Chairman Rogers and Democrat challenger Lee McInnis was not expected to be competitive, and Rogers won handily in Alabama’s solidly Republican 3rd District. Now the big question is whether he seeks a waiver to stay on as HASC’s top Republican.
Rep. Mike Turner vs. Kristina Knickerbocker still undecided: Turner, a longtime HASC member and previous chairman of the House intelligence committee, is still locked in a battle for Ohio’s 10th District against Democratic challenger Kristina Knickerbocker. With 98 percent of the votes counted, Knickerbocker is up by about 1 percent, according to the AP.
Rep. Scott DesJarlais vs. Victoria Broderick still undecided: The AP hasn’t called the race for Tennessee’s Fourth District, which could be an upset if Democrat challenger Victoria Broderick ousts GOP Rep. DesJarlais, who leads HASC’s strategic forces committee. Broderick is up by only a couple fractions of a percentage point.
Rep. Joe Wilson vs. Zyon Khalifa still undecided: Wilson, another longtime HASC member, is still locking horns with Democrat challenger Zyon Khalifa for South Carolina’s 2nd District. Wilson currently leads by 1 percent, according to the AP.
Rep. Jen Kiggans loses to former Rep. Elaine Luria: Former Democratic Rep. Elaine Luria defeated Kiggans, a Republican member of HASC, for Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District. Kiggans is a former Navy helicopter pilot, while Luria is a former naval officer who operated naval reactors onboard warships. Both are strong advocates for shipbuilding.
Rep. Eugene Vindman defeats Douglas Ollivant: Vindman, a Democrat who currently serves on HASC, won a second term representing Virginia’s 7th District after defeating Republican Douglas Ollivant. Both Vindman and Ollivant are retired Army lieutenant colonels who listed veterans’ issues as key priorities.
Rep. Marcy Kaptur defeats Derek Merrin: Kaptur, a Democratic defense appropriator, emerged victorious in Ohio’s 9th District — a seat that Republicans had hoped to flip after recent redistricting made it more GOP-friendly. Kaptur beat Republican Derek Merrin, a former state representative.
Rep. David Valadao vs. Randy Villegas still undecided: The race between Valadao, a Republican on the defense appropriations subcommittee, and Democrat Randy Villegas has not been called. Valadao faces the same conundrum as Kaptur, as California’s 22nd District was recently redrawn and is considered a tossup.
Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart vs. Nicole Locklin still undecided: The AP hasn’t called the race for Florida’s 26th District. With 99 percent of votes in, Diaz-Balart, a House defense appropriator, leads Democrat challenger Nicole Locklin by less than one percent.
Sen. Dan Sullivan vs. former Rep. Mary Peltola still undecided: The Associated Press has not yet called Alaska’s Senate race, with Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, a longtime member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, currently leading by less than a percentage point. Sullivan finds himself embroiled in a four-way race with a strange twist. Not only is he taking on former Rep. Mary Peltola, his Democratic challenger, he also faces an independent candidate who shares his name: former schoolteacher Dan J. Sullivan Jr. The Trump administration has sued to block the certification of the race if a Republican loses, citing name confusion.
Former Rep. Mike Rogers loses to Abdul El-Sayed: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a public health administrator, won the Michigan senate seat. He beat former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican and former chairman of the United States House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.

articles.title: UK airshow RIAT permanently relocates from Fairford
articles.snippet: The new location for the show going forward will be MOD Boscombe Down, roughly 90 minutes south of Fairford by car and equidistant from London
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Royal International Air Tattoo, an annual airshow in the United Kingdom, will permanently move to a new location, organizers announced today.
The decision to shift from RAF Fairford, the air base that has hosted the event for four decades, comes after the 2026 edition of RIAT had to be cancelled due to the use of that airfield for US B-1 bombers operating against Iran. Those bombers were later relocated back to the US due to concerns over a terrorist attack by Iran on the base.
The new location for the show going forward will be MOD Boscombe Down, roughly 90 minutes south of Fairford by car and equidistant from London. The new location “provides an outstanding platform for RIAT’s future ambitions, offering the space, capability and flexibility required to support the event’s continued evolution,” organizers said in a statement.
As a signal of support for RIAT’s organizers, the announcement included comments from Luke Pollard, the minister for Defence Readiness and Industry; Rupert Pearce, the UK’s National Armaments Director; and Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, the Chief of the Air Staff.
“This move secures the future of the airshow for decades into the future and enables the Royal Air Force Charitable Trust’s important work to continue inspiring future generations,” Smyth said in his comments. “The Royal Air Force looks forward to continuing its long-standing partnership with Royal Air Force Charitable Trust Enterprises and supporting future editions of RIAT for many years to come.”
For many years, RIAT was seen as more of a public airshow. However, over the last decade, the defense establishment has increasingly used the event to showcase capabilities and make announcements, sometimes to the detriment of the biennial Farnborough Airshow.
The first RIAT at Boscombe Down is scheduled for July 16-18, 2027.

articles.title: Leonardo, Fincanteri revamp joint venture, aiming to trim frigate build time by 18 months
articles.snippet: Fincantieri CEO Pierroberto Folgiero said his company’s joint venture with Leonardo, the Orrizonte Sistemi Navali, now aims to cut down frigate production time by 18 months.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — Italian defense companies Leonardo and Fincantieri this week announced a restructuring of their Orrizonte Sistemi Navali (OSN) joint venture, which the CEOs of both firms say could trim the time required to build a frigate by 18 months.
The joint venture, which has existed for over two decades, will return to its former model, in which OSN serves as an overarching integrator of an entire warship. The move would effectively change the conglomerate’s current approach, where Fincantieri and Leonardo generally manage separate aspects of the same ship.
The heads of Leonardo and Fincantieri, Lorenzo Mariani and Pierroberto Folgiero, signed a Letter of Intent at the Euronaval defense show here on Tuesday. Executives said the renewed joint venture, in which Fincantieri owns 51 percent and Leonardo 49 percent, would be more competitive in European and export markets.
“Italy has a strong industrial setup in the naval domain, which enables us to perform effectively and deliver faster than in the past. One of OSN’s key objectives will be precisely to shorten these lead times,” Pierroberto Folgiero, the CEO of Fincantieri, told reporters on the sidelines of Euronaval.
Folgiero said executives set a goal of cutting the delivery window for FREMM frigates from 54 to 36 months, a key “test case” that could determine whether the companies’ combined shipbuilding prowess can deliver a vessel on a timeline similar to the Korean industry.
The joint venture’s roster spans several vessel types, including the Italian Navy’s light multirole offshore patrol ship class, the PPX, and the FREMM EVO, an evolution of the Italian Navy’s European Multi-Mission Frigate program.
In September, OSN additionally signed a contract valued at €3.7 billion ($4.2 billion) with OCCAR (Organisation Conjointe de Coopération en matière d’Armement) for the development, production and initial in-service support for two new-generation DDX destroyers to equip the Italian Navy.
In July, Portugal awarded Fincantieri an approximate €3.9 billion ($4.4 billion) order to build three FREMM EVO frigates, with deliveries planned for 2029-2030. In September, Italy and Greece also finalized an agreement to transfer two Carlo Bergamini-class FREMM frigates from the Italian Navy to Athens, where Fincantieri will oversee the technical transfer and modifications of these warships.
Folgiero asserted that Italian Navy ships are “very well-proven at sea” and represent an important benchmark at a time of significant global demand for naval military vessels.
“The ships we have built together with Leonardo for the Italian Navy have a proven track record and are therefore well-positioned to benefit from the increased demand for military naval capabilities worldwide,” he said.

articles.title: Israel Weapons Industry expands into Southeast Asia with Thailand’s deployment of counter-drone system
articles.snippet: “We are seeing strong demand for our platforms and systems across the region,” the company said in response to questions about its growth strategy for southern Asia.”
articles.full_text:
JERUSALEM — Small arms manufacturer Israel Weapons Industry is expanding its reach into Southeast Asia with four nations “currently at different stages of the procurement process” for its ARBEL Anti-Drone System, the company recently told Breaking Defense.
“We are seeing strong demand for our platforms and systems across the region,” the company said in response to questions about its growth strategy for southern Asia, where “countering the growing drone threat is one of the most pressing concerns our customers are raising.”
ARBEL is currently available for AR-15-type platforms, light machine guns and as an anti-drone system. This means soldiers can use it on existing rifle platforms they are already familiar with. It is also “optics-agnostic,” the company noted in an October statement.
Most recently, IWI, which is part of Israel’s SK Group, delivered the ARBEL ADS to Thailand’s Ministry of Defense, the company shared in an Oct. 22 statement.
“Following integration into its existing rifles and on-site training by IWI, the ARBEL ADS has been deployed and is now operational for day and night use,” the company said at the time.
As seen in the Ukraine-Russia war and the conflict between the US and Israel and Iran, small drone threats have been increasing, leading countries to seek out their own drone and counter-drone systems.
In the October statement, SK Group Vice President Doron Korol noted: “As Southeast Asian militaries place greater emphasis on counter-drone capabilities, Thailand’s adoption of ARBEL ADS reflects this growing operational priority. We see rising demand across the region for solutions that can help soldiers meet this challenge.”
SK Group’s Vice Chairman Ronen Hamudot added that “small tactical drones have become a direct and growing threat to soldiers on the battlefield.”
“While each country is moving at its own pace, the level of engagement reflects a broader shift in defense priorities across the region and the growing recognition that counter-drone capabilities are essential to modern military operations,” IWI said in last month’s statement.
Thailand integrated the system by replacing the lower receiver of existing rifles with the Arbel ADS system. “This approach enables militaries to upgrade their existing platforms locally without replacing their rifle inventories or procuring entirely new weapons,” IWI noted in its October statement.
IWI also said there are discussions with Thailand about additional orders.
In response to questions from Breaking Defense, the company said “This year alone, we conducted several ARBEL ADS demonstrations in Southeast Asian countries, reflecting growing interest in effective counter-drone solutions. Thailand’s deployment represents an important milestone, and we see significant potential to build on this momentum across the region.”
The company declined to disclose which other three Asian nations are in the process of procuring ARBEL systems. However, IWI told Breaking Defense that “the threat posed by small tactical drones is not confined to any one region, and Asian militaries face an increasingly complex security environment that includes terrorism, cross-border smuggling and the growing use of drones for hostile attacks.”
The company further pointed to “recent drone-related hostilities along the Cambodia-Thailand border” as underscoring the emerging threats in the region.
IWI unveiled ARBEL in April 2024, and called it the “world’s first-ever revolutionary computerized small arms system” that was “poised to re-defined combat effectiveness.”

articles.title: Ukrainian news outlet Kyiv Independent hit by suspected Russian cyberattack
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: A suspected Russian cyberattack disrupted the website of The Kyiv Independent, one of Ukraine’s leading English-language news outlets.
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian news outlet Kyiv Independent hit by suspected Russian cyberattack
A suspected Russian cyberattack disrupted the website of The Kyiv Independent, one of Ukraine’s leading English-language news outlets, the publication said Wednesday.
The hackers gained access to the outlet’s website management system and a service used to distribute newsletters, allowing them to publish false messages and send emails to subscribers in Russian and English.
One of the malicious emails falsely claimed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had launched a nuclear warhead at Kyiv as a “proof of friendship” following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The message, written in Russian, urged recipients to seek shelter and included the username of an anonymous Telegram channel.
Other emails included fabricated claims about a physical attack on Zelensky. The hackers also posted messages on the publication’s website, which staff quickly removed.
The Kyiv Independent attributed the attack to suspected Russian actors based on the content of the messages, although it did not provide technical evidence linking the breach to Moscow.
“Attacks like these are part of the war we cover every day — an attempt to sow confusion and erode trust,” said Editor-in-Chief Olga Rudenko.
This is the first time the publication has faced an attack of this kind, Rudenko said.
The Kyiv Independent, founded in November 2021, has become a prominent source of English-language reporting on Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The outlet said it attracted nearly 3 million monthly readers in 2025, most of them outside Ukraine, and has more than 35,000 paying members who help finance its operations. The Kyiv Independent also operates an investigative unit that documents alleged Russian war crimes.
The publication said its members’ and donors’ banking information was not compromised because payments are processed through secure third-party services.
Its staff are working with cybersecurity specialists to investigate the breach, identify vulnerabilities and prevent further intrusions, according to chief operating officer Zakhar Protsiuk.
“This attack won’t stop us from doing our work,” Protsiuk said.
The incident comes just days after hackers compromised Ukraine’s widely used air raid alert app, sending fabricated warnings about nuclear and chemical threats and street fighting.
One of the fake alerts warned of a possible strike involving Russia’s nuclear-capable Oreshnik ballistic missile and directed users to a Telegram channel associated with a previously unknown hacking group calling itself Hitcore Corp. There is no confirmed connection between the two incidents.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Cyberattack wipes cloud data at major Russian hosting provider Beget
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: A major Russian web hosting provider is struggling to restore its services after a cyberattack destroyed data across its cloud infrastructure and disrupted hundreds of websites.
articles.full_text:
Cyberattack wipes cloud data at major Russian hosting provider Beget
A major Russian web hosting provider is struggling to restore its services after a cyberattack destroyed data across its cloud infrastructure and disrupted hundreds of websites.
Beget, one of Russia's largest domain registrars and hosting companies, said Wednesday that it had begun bringing some servers back online following the attack, which took place overnight on Sunday.
"Restoring all services will take a considerable amount of time, as more than 1,000 servers must be manually inspected," the company said.
According to Beget's statement, the attackers gained access to systems used to manage the company's infrastructure, allowing them to execute scripts designed to erase data.
